items.title: Government Silence Regarding Christodoulides’ Proposal for Varosha
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – The government in Nicosia neither confirmed nor denied a report in the newspaper Phileleftheros that President Nikos Christodoulides has submitted a proposal to open Varosha under UN administration in exchange for the operation of the port of Famagusta under EU supervision. The director of the President’s Press Office, Victoras Papadopoulos, in statements to the state broadcaster RIK, confined himself to recalling that President Christodoulides had submitted 19 proposals on different issues during the leaders’ last meeting, on September 17, the contents of which, he said, he could not disclose in order to protect the peace effort currently underway. Even the mayor of occupied Famagusta, Simos Ioannou, said he was unaware that such a proposal had been submitted, stressing, however, that he had long been asking the government to submit a proposal for Varosha and that the President had committed to doing so at a meeting held approximately two months ago.

items.title: Marco Rubio in Athens for U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue: Defense, energy, regional security high on the agenda
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS - U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in Athens late Tuesday for the sixth round of the U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, landing at Athens International Airport at approximately 9:20 p.m. and being received by Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis. Rubio’s visit comes as the two allies seek to further deepen their cooperation in defense, energy and regional security, with the agenda also covering shipping, technology, trade and investment. Before arriving in Athens, Rubio described Greece as a “very important ally” of the United States. On defense, particular emphasis is expected to be placed on further strengthening U.S.-Greek military cooperation, including the F-35 program and the upgrade of Greece’s F-16 fleet to the Viper configuration. The talks are also expected to address the procurement of additional U.S. weapons systems and support for existing American-made equipment operated by the Greek armed forces.

The "Maran Gas Mystras", with a capacity of 159,800 cubic metres, was built in 2015 and is owned by the Angelicoussis Shipping Group.

Speaking to ERT television, Papastavrou said Greece and other countries in the region have the infrastructure needed to serve as a key transit route for replacing Russian gas supplies. “The Vertical Corridor strengthens Greece’s role in the region while reducing the energy influence of Turkey and Russia,” Papastavrou said. “That is the reality. And that is why it is so important for all of us to understand the geopolitical significance that the success of the Vertical Corridor has for our country.”

items.title: US supreme court to hear big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuits
items.summary_raw:
Court starts new term hearing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level

The US supreme court begins its new nine-month term hearing arguments Monday in a high-stakes case in which big oil companies are attempting to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for the climate crisis.

In Suncor Energy versus the County Commissioners of Boulder County, local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that climate change has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Canada-based Suncor are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit.

Australia had its second hottest September on record last month as global heating and a strengthening El Niño combined to break a string of heat records around the country.

Bureau of Meteorology data showed the minimum night-time temperatures across the continent were also the hottest for any September, on a record that goes back to 1910. Averaged temperatures ranked in the top five warmest Septembers for every state, and the sixth hottest for the Northern Territory.

items.title: Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coal
items.summary_raw:
Global campaign group 350.org urges Cop31 hosts to announce a coal phase-out date and national roadmaps to get off fossil fuels

  • Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

The hosts of the next major United Nations climate conference, Turkey and Australia, are facing criticism for being partners in a coal supply chain while remaining near silent on the need for a global deal to rapidly get off fossil fuels.

With the Cop31 summit in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya just a month away, the two countries running the fortnight-long talks have been accused by activists of a “vacuum of action” on plans for a transition away from coal, gas and oil – a key goal of many nations at the talks.

items.title: The expansion of Heathrow would be an expensive disaster for Britain and the world. Burnham needs to block it | George Monbiot
items.summary_raw:
A third runway would fly in the face of reason. If we are to prioritise human life over short-term ‘growth’, we need to use planes less, not more


If a third runway is built at Heathrow, what will be the impact on the wealth of the nation? It will cost us somewhere between £23.4bn and £62.5bn. These are not my figures; they weren’t calculated by environmental groups, but by the Department for Transport.

For decades, government ministers have told us that airport expansion is essential for “growth”. As chancellor, Rachel Reeves claimed that a third runway at Heathrow would add 0.43% to GDP, figures we later discovered came from a report commissioned by the airport. items.summary_raw: OSINTdefender The U.S. military has sent additional Patriot air defense missile batteries to protect oil and gas facilities in Saudi Arabia and Qatar, according to two U.S. officials and a regional source who spoke to Axios. One battery went to a Saudi oil facility, another to a Qatari gas facility, officials say the move is meant to reassure both allies their energy infrastructure will be protected if President Trump resumes major strikes on Iran. Officials from U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) declined to comment.  President Donald J. Trump said Thursday he's weighing renewed bombing in the coming weeks: "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer." Officials say Saudi and Qatari leaders lobbied Trump in August against striking Iranian energy infrastructure, warning of retaliation against their own facilities, and that this was a key reason he pulled back toward economic pressure instead at the time. The U.S. is expected to need Saudi airspace access for any renewed operations. items.title: Eastern Spain braces for torrential rain and flooding
items.summary_raw:
Up to 300mm of rain could fall in places, while extreme downpours bring landslides and deaths in Nepal

Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.

Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.

items.title: The New York Times, citing a Russian document allegedly intercepted by Ukraine, reports that Russia intends to use up to 1,000 drones, missiles, and glide-bombs against Ukrainian e…
items.summary_raw: The New York Times, citing a Russian document allegedly intercepted by Ukraine, reports that Russia intends to use up to 1,000 drones, missiles, and glide-bombs against Ukrainian energy and water infrastructure in winter, especially in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa. Russia will also reportedly target the electrical switchyards at the Rivne, Khmelnytskyi, and South-Ukraine Nuclear Power Plants.   In Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa, Russia reportedly plans to cut electricity and heating by 90%, while causing significant disruption to their water sewerage system. The strike campaign will reportedly take place in three stages, starting with targeting electrical substation near the western borders of Ukraine used to transfer European-supplies electricity, before moving to hydro-electric power plants, and then targeting nuclear power plants at the end.   In my opinion, 1,000 missiles, drones, and glide-bombs is a massive undercount. According to available information, Russia has over 12,000 Geran-2 drones in reserve, a portion of which they will likely use during the winter for strikes on energy targets. items.title: May heatwaves, deaths, ruined harvests: study of Europe’s summer paints grim picture for the future
items.summary_raw:
EU Copernicus report shows surface air temperatures from June to August were 2.5C above decadal average

The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, a report has found, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C.

Surface air temperatures in western Europe from June to August were 2.5C above the recent decadal average, according to an update from the EU’s Copernicus climate monitoring service on Friday, while milder but still deadly heat across the rest of the continent made the summer Europe’s third hottest on record.

items.summary_raw: Visioner BIG | 🇷🇺🇪🇪‼️‼️ Russia has stopped a Western-owned commercial vessel in the Baltic Sea in what Estonian authorities describe as the first such incident linked to retaliation over sanctions targeting Moscow’s shadow fleet.  The Cyprus-flagged cargo ship Västerbotten departed Sweden on September 29 and was due to arrive in Estonia on October 1. After entering Russian territorial waters, it was stopped and ordered to anchor in the Gulf of Finland. Russian border guards inspected the vessel for several hours before allowing it to continue toward Estonia.  The vessel’s eventual release kept the incident from developing into a larger confrontation, but the detention adds a new maritime dimension to tensions in the Baltic. If such actions become more frequent, commercial shipping could increasingly find itself caught in the broader sanctions confrontation between Russia and European states.  See the latest updates with us: @visionergeo tweet

Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. They argue that “gutting one of the country’s most significant climate protections” will set the nation back decades and worsen the climate crisis.

items.title: New Tensions with Ankara over Greece-Cyprus Electricity Cable
items.summary_raw:
ATHENS - The Greece-Cyprus electricity interconnection project is entering a new phase of tension, with Ankara insisting that it will not allow the cable to be laid without prior Turkish authorization, while Athens categorically rejects the demand, citing international law and the Law of the Sea. Turkey’s Defense Ministry, in a new statement, reiterated that it will not permit cable-laying work without Turkey’s approval, arguing that part of the planned survey activity will take place in an area that Ankara considers to be part of the Turkish continental shelf. The Greek government, for its part, insists that no Turkish authorization is required. Government spokesperson Pavlos Marinakis has said that “there is no issue of authorization” and that the project will proceed on the basis of international law. “We will not rewrite international law because one country does not like it,” he said.

The post New Tensions with Ankara over Greece-Cyprus Electricity Cable appeared first on The National Herald.

items.title: 66th Anniversary of the Republic of Cyprus’ Independence Honored with Splendor
items.summary_raw:
NICOSIA – The 66th anniversary of the proclamation of the Republic of Cyprus was celebrated with great splendor, including a large military parade in Nicosia. Attention centered on the National Guard’s new weapons systems, the flyovers by Greek F-16 fighter aircraft, and the presence of military contingents from five countries. The presence of modern missile, anti-aircraft, and unmanned systems reflected the modernization of the National Guard’s arsenal and the significant upgrading of the Cypriot military’s operational capabilities in recent years. A special moment that stirred deep emotion was the appearance in the skies over Nicosia of Greek F-16 Vipers, which took off from the ‘Andreas Papandreou’ air base in Paphos. The F-16 Vipers, which flew at low altitude over Iosif Hadjiiosif Avenue, where the parade took place, are the most modern upgraded version of the F-16s operated by the Hellenic Air Force. They are equipped with advanced AESA radar, a new mission computer, and upgraded communications systems.

items.title: ‘Explosion of melt rates’: 20% of Swiss glaciers lost in five years
items.summary_raw:
Alpine regions in Europe experiencing extreme glacier collapse due to heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution

Switzerland has lost almost one-fifth of its ice in just five years, research has found, in a dramatic reshaping of the Alpine country whose big white glaciers have been reduced to moonlike rock deserts, scientists say.

Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%.

items.summary_raw:
Study says UK-based banks provided $8.3bn in coal financing in four years, with Barclays and HSBC leading rise

UK banks are Europe’s biggest financial backers of the global coal industry, providing billions of pounds in funding for the climate-wrecking fossil fuel in the past four years, according to a report.

The study found UK-based banks had provided $8.3bn (£6.2bn) in coal financing since Cop26 in Glasgow in 2021, when global leaders pledged to “phase down” coal use. This compared with $4.9bn from German banks and $3.4bn from French banks over the same period.

items.summary_raw:
Wave nearing southern California expected to reach San Francisco Bay Area by October as it crawls toward Alaska

Communities across California are rushing to prepare for the imminent arrival of the so-called “Kelvin wave”, a massive underwater band of warm water threatening to inundate swaths of the vast North American shoreline.

The wave is nearing southern California and expected to reach the San Francisco Bay Area by early October, as it crawls toward Alaska. Waters could rise by a foot along the California coast, according to scientists, who have warned that this could dramatically double the 8-12in rise in sea levels already caused by climate change over the last century.

items.title: Libya's secret executions: Why now?
items.summary_raw:
Libya's secret executions: Why now?

At least 30 men have been executed in eastern Libya after being sentenced to death in secret military trials by the Libyan Armed Forces, under commander Khalifa Haftar, for the first time since 2010.

Human Rights Watch's Ahmed Benchemsi tells Mathilda Mallinson on MEE Live that the executions have been able to go ahead now due to lack of accountability against actors in the region and international actors with interests in Libyan factions.
